My first pottery bowl leaned to one side. The teacher's bowl was smooth and round. Mine looked worse whenever I (1) ____ them. I wanted to throw it away.

Ms Green asked what I had planned to do with it. “Give it to my brother,” I said. He had moved away to study, and I wanted him to have something from home. “Don't judge its value only by its (2) ____,” she replied.

A deep thumb mark remained where I had lifted the clay too early. Ms Green showed me how to smooth it. The clay was still (3) ____, so pressing hard would change its shape. I worked slowly until only a faint line remained.

After firing, the bowl was hard but still uneven. I painted it blue, my brother's (4) ____. He always chose blue clothes and bags. Inside, I drew our dog. That detail made it (5) ____ from the other bowls.

My brother sent me a photograph after receiving it. The bowl held paper clips on his desk. He had found a practical (6) ____ for it instead of merely displaying it.

I could see the uneven edge. The bowl had not suddenly become (7) ____. Yet I no longer wanted to hide it. By focusing on mistakes, I had almost (8) ____ the person it was for. I kept my next bowl, too, hoping to improve it without (9) ____ everything that made it mine. Learning could include (10) ____ work I was still learning from.

completed_passage:
My first pottery bowl leaned to one side. The teacher's bowl was smooth and round. Mine looked worse whenever I compared them. I wanted to throw it away.

Ms Green asked what I had planned to do with it. “Give it to my brother,” I said. He had moved away to study, and I wanted him to have something from home. “Don't judge its value only by its appearance,” she replied.

A deep thumb mark remained where I had lifted the clay too early. Ms Green showed me how to smooth it. The clay was still soft, so pressing hard would change its shape. I worked slowly until only a faint line remained.

After firing, the bowl was hard but still uneven. I painted it blue, my brother's favourite. He always chose blue clothes and bags. Inside, I drew our dog. That detail made it different from the other bowls.

My brother sent me a photograph after receiving it. The bowl held paper clips on his desk. He had found a practical use for it instead of merely displaying it.

I could see the uneven edge. The bowl had not suddenly become perfect. Yet I no longer wanted to hide it. By focusing on mistakes, I had almost forgotten the person it was for. I kept my next bowl, too, hoping to improve it without removing everything that made it mine. Learning could include keeping work I was still learning from.
